data_points.claim: Over 70% of introductory physics students enter class believing a continuous force is necessary to maintain constant velocity.
Newton's Third Law force pairs act on two separate interacting objects and never cancel each other out on a single object.
data_points.source_name: The Physics Classroom - Newton's Third Law Analysis

data_points.claim: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass; doubling the mass of an object halves its acceleration under the same net force (a = F/m).

common_questions: Why does a book stop sliding across a table if no one touches it?
If every action has an equal opposite reaction, how does anything ever accelerate?
What is the difference between velocity and acceleration in F=ma?

misconceptions.myth: Objects naturally slow down because their force runs out.
misconceptions.reality: Objects slow down only because an external unbalanced force (friction/air resistance) acts on them. In deep space, motion continues forever without engine thrust.

misconceptions.myth: In a collision between a truck and a bug, the truck exerts a bigger force on the bug than the bug exerts on the truck.
misconceptions.reality: Both exert the exact same magnitude of force on each other; the bug experiences massive acceleration due to its microscopic mass (a = F/m).

research_summary: Newton's laws of motion are often taught as dry formulas, but students struggle because their everyday experience of friction conflicts with the laws of inertia and action-reaction. A whiteboard-style explainer that visually exposes the 'hidden force of friction' and diagrams vector pairs on separate bodies bridges intuitive misconceptions with rigorous physics.
